paragraphs: The argument was over. But oddly enough, Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had been in such good spirits, suddenly started to scowl. He scowled and gulped brandy, and that glass was already one too many.

“Clear out, you Jesuits!” he shouted at the servants. “Go away, Smerdyakov. I’ll send you that gold piece I promised you today, but get out! Don’t cry, Grigory. Go to Marfa. She’ll comfort you and put you to bed. These rascals won’t even leave us in peace after dinner,” he snapped peevishly, while the servants hurried out at his word.
“Smerdyakov always shoves his way in now, after dinner. It’s you he’s so keen on. What have you done to charm him?” he added, to Ivan.
“Nothing at all,” answered Ivan. “He likes to think highly of me. He’s a lackey and a mean soul. But he’s raw material for a revolution, when the time comes.”
“A revolution?”
“There will be others, and better ones. But there’ll be some like him as well. His sort will come first, and the better ones after.”
“And when will that time come?”
“The rocket may go up and just fizzle out. So far the peasants don’t much like listening to these soup-makers.”
“Ah, brother, but a Balaam’s ass like that thinks and thinks, and the devil only knows where he ends up.”
“He’s storing up ideas,” said Ivan, with a smile.

“Look, I know he can’t bear me, or anybody else, even you, though you imagine he thinks highly of you. With Alyosha it’s worse: he despises Alyosha. But he doesn’t steal, I’ll say that for him, and he’s no gossip. He keeps quiet and doesn’t air our dirty linen in public. And he makes first-rate fish pasties. But damn him, is he worth all this talk?”
“Of course he isn’t.”

“And as for whatever ideas he’s hatching, the Russian peasant, generally speaking, needs a good thrashing. I’ve always said so. Our peasants are swindlers, they don’t deserve any pity, and it’s a good thing they still get flogged now and then. Russia is rich in birches. If they cut down the forests, Russia would be ruined. I stand up for the clever people. We’ve given up thrashing the peasants, we’ve got so clever, but they keep right on thrashing themselves. And a good thing too. ‘For with what measure ye mete it shall be measured to you again,’ or how does it go? Anyway, it will be measured out. But Russia is all swinishness. My dear boy, if you only knew how I hate Russia.... That is, not Russia, but all this vice! But maybe I do mean Russia. _Tout cela c’est de la cochonnerie_.... Do you know what I like? I like wit.”
“You’ve had another glass. That’s enough.”

“Hold on a minute. I’ll have one more, then another, and then I’ll stop. No, wait, you cut me off. At Mokroe I got talking to an old man, and he said to me: ‘What we like best of all is sentencing the girls to a thrashing, and we always hand the job to the lads. Then the girl he thrashes today, the young fellow asks to marry tomorrow. So the girls are quite happy with it too,’ he said. A fine set of de Sades, eh? But it’s clever, all the same. Shall we drive over and take a look, eh? Alyosha, are you blushing? Don’t be shy, child. What a pity I didn’t stay for dinner at the Superior’s and tell the monks about the girls at Mokroe. Alyosha, don’t be angry that I insulted your Superior this morning. I lost my temper. If there is a God, if He exists, then of course I’m to blame, and I’ll have to answer for it. But if there’s no God at all, what do they deserve, those fathers of yours? Cutting off their heads wouldn’t be enough, since they hold back progress. Will you believe, Ivan, that it lacerates my feelings? No, you won’t, I can see it in your eyes. You believe what people say, that I’m nothing but a buffoon. Alyosha, do you believe I’m nothing but a buffoon?”
“No, I don’t believe that.”

“And I believe you don’t, and that you’re telling the truth. You look honest and you speak honestly. Not Ivan, though. Ivan is stuck-up.... All the same, I’d finish off your monks. I’d take all that mystic stuff and stamp it out, once and for all, across the whole of Russia, to bring every fool to his senses. And think of all the gold and silver that would pour into the mint!”
“But why stamp it out?” asked Ivan.
“So that Truth can win. That’s why.”
“Well, if Truth did win, you know, you’d be the first one to be robbed and stamped out.”

“Ah! You may well be right. Ah, what an ass I am!” burst out Fyodor Pavlovitch, giving his forehead a light slap. “Very well, then, your monastery can stay, Alyosha, if that’s how it is. And we clever people will sit comfortable and enjoy our brandy. You know, Ivan, the Almighty Himself must have arranged it that way. Ivan, tell me, is there a God or not? No, wait, tell the truth, tell it seriously. Why are you laughing again?”
“I’m laughing at the clever remark you made just now, about Smerdyakov believing in those two saints who could move mountains.”
“What, am I like him now?”
“Very much so.”

“Well, that proves I’m a Russian too, with a Russian trait. And you can be caught the same way, philosopher or not. Shall I catch you? What do you bet I’ll catch you tomorrow? Tell me anyway, is there a God or not? Only be serious. I want you serious now.”
“No, there is no God.”
“Alyosha, is there a God?”
“There is.”
“Ivan, and is there some kind of immortality, just a little, just a tiny bit?”
“There’s no immortality either.”
“None at all?”
“None at all.”
“Then it’s absolute nothingness. But maybe there’s just something? Anything is better than nothing!”
“Absolute nothingness.”
“Alyosha, is there immortality?”
“There is.”
“God and immortality?”
“God and immortality. Immortality is in God.”

“H’m! Ivan is probably right. Good Lord! Think of all the faith, all the strength of every kind, that man has poured into that dream for nothing, and for so many thousands of years. Who is it that laughs at man? Ivan! One last time, once and for all, is there a God or not? I’m asking for the last time!”
“And for the last time, there is not.”
“Then who is laughing at mankind, Ivan?”
“It must be the devil,” said Ivan, with a smile.
“And the devil? Is there one?”
“No, there’s no devil either.”
“What a shame. Damn it all, what I wouldn’t do to the man who first thought up God! Hanging from a bitter aspen would be too good for him.”
“There’d have been no civilization if they hadn’t thought up God.”
“There wouldn’t? Without God?”
“No. And no brandy either. Still, I’m going to take your brandy away from you.”
“Stop, stop, stop, my dear boy, just one more little glass. I’ve hurt Alyosha’s feelings. You’re not angry with me, Alyosha? My dear little Alexey!”
“No, I’m not angry. I know how you think. Your heart is better than your head.”
“My heart is better than my head, is it? Oh, Lord! And coming from you. Ivan, do you love Alyosha?”
“Yes.”

“You must love him” (Fyodor Pavlovitch was by now very drunk). “Listen, Alyosha, I was rude to your elder this morning. But I was all stirred up. Still, that elder has some wit, don’t you think, Ivan?”
“Quite possibly.”

“He has, he has. _Il y a du Piron là-dedans._ He’s a Jesuit, a Russian one, that is. He’s an honorable man, so there’s a hidden indignation seething in him at having to put on an act and play the holy man.”
“But surely he does believe in God.”

“Not a bit. Didn’t you know? Why, he says so himself, to everyone. That is, not everyone, but all the clever people who go to see him. He told Governor Schultz to his face, not long ago: ‘_Credo_, but I don’t know in what.’”
“Really?”

“He really did. But I respect him. There’s something of Mephistopheles in him, or rather of ‘The Hero of Our Time’ ... Arbenin, or whatever his name is?... You see, he’s a sensualist. He’s such a sensualist that I’d fear for my daughter or my wife if she went to confess to him. You know, when he starts telling stories.... The year before last he asked us to tea, tea with liqueur (the ladies send him liqueur), and began telling us about the old days until we nearly split our sides.... Especially how he once cured a paralyzed woman. ‘If my legs weren’t bad, I know a dance I could show you,’ he said. What do you make of that? ‘I’ve played plenty of tricks in my day,’ said he. He swindled Dernidov, the merchant, out of sixty thousand.”
“What, he stole it?”

“The merchant brought him the money, as to a man he could trust, and said, ‘Keep it for me, friend, the police are searching my place tomorrow.’ And he kept it. ‘You gave it to the Church,’ he declared. I said to him: ‘You’re a scoundrel,’ I said. ‘No,’ said he, ‘I’m not a scoundrel, I’m broad-minded.’ But that wasn’t him, that was somebody else. I’ve mixed him up with somebody else ... and never noticed. Come on, one more glass and that’s all. Take the bottle away, Ivan. I’ve been telling lies. Why didn’t you stop me, Ivan, and tell me I was lying?”
“I knew you’d stop on your own.”
“That’s a lie. You did it out of spite, plain spite against me. You despise me. You came into my house and despised me under my own roof.”
“Well, I’m leaving. You’ve had too much brandy.”
“I begged you, for Christ’s sake, to go to Tchermashnya for a day or two, and you won’t go.”
“I’ll go tomorrow, if you’re so set on it.”
“You won’t go. You want to keep an eye on me. That’s what you’re after, you spiteful fellow. That’s why you won’t go.”
The old man would not let it drop. He had reached the stage of drunkenness where a drunkard who has been quiet until then starts picking a quarrel and trying to throw his weight around.

“What are you staring at me for? Why do you look like that? Your eyes look at me and say, ‘You ugly drunk!’ Your eyes don’t trust me. They’re full of contempt.... You’ve come here with some plan in mind. Now Alyosha looks at me and his eyes shine. Alyosha doesn’t despise me. Alexey, you mustn’t love Ivan.”
“Don’t be nasty to my brother. Stop going after him,” Alyosha said firmly.
“Oh, all right. Ugh, my head aches. Take the brandy away, Ivan. That’s the third time I’m telling you.”
He brooded for a moment, and then a slow, sly grin crept over his face.

“Don’t be angry with a feeble old man, Ivan. I know you don’t love me, but don’t be angry anyway. You’ve got nothing to love me for. You go to Tchermashnya. I’ll come out to you myself and bring you a present. I’ll show you a little wench there. I’ve had my eye on her for a long time. She still runs around barefoot. Don’t be scared of barefoot wenches—don’t despise them—they’re pearls!”
And he kissed his hand with a loud smack.

“To my mind,” he came to life at once, seeming to sober up the moment he touched on his favorite subject. “To my mind ... Ah, you boys! You children, you little sucking-pigs, to my mind ... I have never in my life found a woman ugly—that’s been my rule! Can you grasp that? How could you grasp it? There’s milk in your veins, not blood. You haven’t crawled out of your shells yet. My rule has always been that in every woman you can find something devilishly interesting that you won’t find in any other. You just have to know how to find it, that’s the point! That’s a talent! To my mind there are no ugly women. The mere fact that she’s a woman is half the battle ... but how could you grasp that? Even in _vieilles filles_, even in them you can find something that makes you wonder how men could be such fools as to let them grow old without noticing them. Barefoot girls and plain ones, you have to take by surprise. Didn’t you know that? You have to astonish them until they’re enchanted, thrown, ashamed that a gentleman like you should fall in love with a little slut like them. It’s a jolly good thing that there always are, and always will be, masters and slaves in the world. So there will always be a little maid-of-all-work and her master, and you know, that’s all anyone needs for happiness. Wait ... listen, Alyosha, I always used to surprise your mother too, but in a different way. I paid her no attention at all, and then all at once, when the moment came, I’d be devotion itself, crawling on my knees, kissing her feet, and I always, always—I remember it as if it were today—brought her to that tinkling, quiet, nervous, queer little laugh. It was hers alone. I knew her attacks always began that way. The next day she’d start shrieking in hysterics, and this little laugh was no sign of delight, though it made a very good fake. That’s the great thing, knowing how to handle each person. Once Belyavsky—a handsome fellow, and rich—used to like coming here and hanging around her—suddenly gave me a slap in the face in front of her. And she—such a mild sheep—why, I thought she’d knock me down for that blow. How she went for me! ‘You’re beaten, beaten now,’ she said. ‘You took a blow from him. You’ve been trying to sell me to him,’ she said.... ‘And how dared he hit you in front of me! Don’t you ever come near me again, never, never! Run at once, challenge him to a duel!’... So then I took her to the monastery to bring her to her senses. The holy Fathers prayed her back to reason. But I swear by God, Alyosha, I never insulted the poor crazy girl! Only once, maybe, in the first year; she was very fond of praying then. She kept the feasts of Our Lady above all, and on those days she’d throw me out of her room. I’ll knock that mysticism out of her, I thought! ‘Look,’ I said, ‘here’s your holy image. Here it is. See, I’m taking it down. You believe it works miracles, but watch, I’ll spit on it this minute and nothing will happen to me for it!’... When she saw that, good Lord! I thought she’d kill me. But all she did was jump up and wring her hands, then suddenly cover her face with them, start trembling all over, and drop to the floor ... dropped all in a heap. Alyosha, Alyosha, what’s the matter?”

The old man leaped up in alarm. From the time he began talking about Alyosha’s mother, a change had been coming over Alyosha’s face little by little. He had flushed crimson, his eyes glowed, his lips trembled. The old sot had gone spluttering on without noticing anything, until something very strange happened to Alyosha. Exactly what he was describing in the crazy woman was suddenly happening again in Alyosha. He sprang up from his seat just as his mother was said to have done, wrung his hands, hid his face in them, and fell back into his chair, shaking all over in a hysterical fit of sudden, violent, silent weeping. His extraordinary likeness to his mother struck the old man especially.

“Ivan, Ivan! Water, quick! It’s just like her, exactly how she used to be then, his mother. Spit some water over him from your mouth, that’s what I used to do with her. He’s upset about his mother, his mother,” he muttered to Ivan.

“But she was my mother too, I believe, his mother. Wasn’t she?” said Ivan, in uncontrolled anger and contempt. The old man cringed before his blazing eyes. But something very strange had happened, though only for a second: it really seemed to have slipped the old man’s mind that Alyosha’s mother was in fact Ivan’s mother as well.

“Your mother?” he muttered, not understanding. “What do you mean? What mother are you talking about? Was she?... Why, damn it! Of course she was yours too! Damn it! My mind has never been so clouded before. Forgive me, why, I was thinking, Ivan.... He he he!” He broke off. A broad, drunken, half-witless grin spread across his face.
At that moment a dreadful din and uproar broke out in the hall. There were violent shouts, the door was flung open, and Dmitri burst into the room. The old man ran to Ivan in terror.
“He’ll kill me! He’ll kill me! Don’t let him get at me!” he screamed, clutching the tail of Ivan’s coat.
